pos: adj. (comparative of weighty; of greater importance)
etymology: From weight, Saxon wiht, with the comparative ending. In Matthew 23:23 it renders the Greek barutera, from barus, heavy.
biblical_def: The fourth woe on the scribes and Pharisees is the one that exposes their whole method: “Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone” (Matthew 23:23). The Lord grants the tithing of garden herbs — not to leave the other undone — and then names three things they had dropped: judgment, mercy, and faith. The Greek is the word for heavy. The law has weight in it, and not every precept weighs the same. This is not a liberal release from the law's details; it is the Lawgiver's own ordering of His own commandments, and it answers Micah 6:8 word for word — do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with thy God. The next verse gives the image: “Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel” (Matthew 23:24). A man can be scrupulous about herbs and carry a camel down his throat. The dictionary notes that this is the characteristic hypocrisy of the religiously meticulous, and that Christ, not the modern critic, is the one who said it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): WEIGHTY, adjective Having great weight; heavy; also, important; momentous; as weighty matters.
webster_full: WEIGHTY, adjective Having great weight; heavy; ponderous.
2. Important; momentous; as a weighty consideration.
3. Rigorous; severe; as a weighty sentence.
WEIGHTILY, adverb Heavily; ponderously; with force; solidly.
WEIGHTINESS, noun Ponderousness; gravity; heaviness; also, solidity; force; importance.
scriptures: ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.

Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: The verse is used to excuse neglect of the law's details; Christ said the lighter things ought to have been done too.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 23:23 is the favourite proof-text of everyone who wants the commandments ranked so that his own neglect lands in the light end. Christ forecloses that: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. He does not release the Pharisees from tithing mint; He condemns them for tithing mint while dropping judgment, mercy, and faith.

The principle to recover is that the Lawgiver weighs His own law, and we do not. Judgment, mercy, and faith are heavier than cummin because He says so. A man who decides for himself which commands are weighty has simply chosen a different set of herbs to be scrupulous about.

pos: adj. (comparative of sore; more grievous, more severe)
etymology: Saxon sar, grievous, painful, with the comparative ending. In Hebrews 10:29 it renders the Greek cheirona, worse.
biblical_def: The writer to the Hebrews has just said that a man who despised Moses' law died without mercy, and then presses the argument upward: “Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?” (Hebrews 10:29). Three charges, each worse than the last: the Son trodden under foot, His blood called unholy, the Spirit of grace insulted. The Authorized Version uses sorer once, and the whole weight of the epistle's warning passages rests on this comparative. Greater light brings greater guilt. The context is wilful sin after receiving the knowledge of the truth (Hebrews 10:26), and the dictionary reads these warnings as Scripture gives them — addressed to professors, meant to be felt, and perfectly consistent with the perseverance of the saints. Those who truly belong to Christ are kept, and one of the means by which they are kept is this warning. The apostate who finally tramples the Son was never sanctified by that blood in the saving sense; the warning is nonetheless real, and Hebrews 2:3 asks the same question of every hearer: how shall we escape?
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SORE, adjective Tender and painful; severe; afflictive; distressing. Comparative, sorer.
webster_full: SORE, adjective Tender and painful; susceptible of pain from pressure.
2. Severe; violent; afflictive; as a sore famine.
3. Criminal; evil; as a sore fault.
SORELY, adverb With violent pain and distress; grievously; greatly.
SORENESS, noun The tenderness of any part of an animal body.
scriptures: Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace?
For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins,
Heb 2:3
How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation; which at the first began to be spoken by the Lord, and was confirmed unto us by them that heard him;
corruption_summary: Hebrews 10:29 is used either to deny perseverance or to deny eternal punishment; it does neither, and it is not softened.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions pull at this verse. Arminian readings make it proof that a regenerate man may be finally lost; annihilationist and universalist readings empty the punishment of its eternity. The dictionary holds the Reformed position: the elect are kept by the power of God and shall not finally fall, and the punishment of the impenitent is eternal and conscious. The warning is addressed to professors precisely because profession is not possession.

The principle to recover is that light increases accountability. Despising Moses brought death; treading under foot the Son of God brings worse. This is the logic the epistle uses from chapter 2 to chapter 12, and it is the ground of every faithful appeal to a congregation that has heard the gospel and not obeyed it.

pos: adj. (comparative of vile; baser, more worthless)
etymology: Latin vilis, cheap, of small value, through French vil. In Job 30:8 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning struck out or driven from the land.
biblical_def: Job's lament in chapter 30 turns on a reversal of station: “But now they that are younger than I have me in derision, whose fathers I would have disdained to have set with the dogs of my flock” (Job 30:1). The men now mocking him are the sons of outcasts: “They were children of fools, yea, children of base men: they were viler than the earth” (Job 30:8). The Authorized Version uses viler once. It is a hard verse and the dictionary does not flinch from what it says: Job, an upright man, is describing his humiliation by reciting the worthlessness of his mockers. Scripture records the complaint without endorsing every judgment in it — Job will be corrected out of the whirlwind for what he said about God, though not for what he said about his tormentors. The word vile in Scripture is almost always a judgment on character rather than on station. Job uses it of men driven out of the land for their crimes. And the same man who said this says of himself, when God finally speaks: I am vile; I will lay mine hand upon my mouth. The lesson runs both ways, and the second direction is the one that matters.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): VILE, adjective Base; mean; worthless; despicable; morally base; sinful. Comparative, viler.
webster_full: VILE, adjective Base; mean; worthless; despicable.
2. Morally base or impure; sinful; depraved by sin; wicked.

2. Moral baseness or depravity; degeneracy.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors handle this verse badly. The first quotes Job 30:8 as though Scripture endorsed contempt for the poor; it does not, and the law of Moses is full of provision for the stranger and the fatherless. The second treats the whole chapter as sub-Christian and discards it; but it is canonical lament, and the Holy Spirit recorded a suffering man's words as he said them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in Job 40:4. The man who called his mockers viler than the earth said of himself, before God, I am vile, and laid his hand on his mouth. That is the end of all comparison.

pos: adj. (comparative of poor; of less means)
etymology: Latin pauper, poor, through French povre, with the comparative ending. In Leviticus 27:8 it renders a Hebrew word for being low or brought down.
biblical_def: Leviticus 27 sets a scale of values for persons devoted to the LORD by a singular vow, and then makes express provision for the man who cannot pay it: “But if he be poorer than thy estimation, then he shall present himself before the priest, and the priest shall value him; according to his ability that vowed shall the priest value him” (Leviticus 27:8). The Authorized Version uses poorer once, and it is in a mercy clause. The fixed scale stood; the poor man was not excluded from it; the priest assessed him according to his ability. Nothing in the chapter lowers the standard, and nothing in it bars the man without means. The same principle runs through the sacrificial law — a bullock, or a lamb, or two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, according to what a worshipper could bring — and it is why Mary and Joseph offered birds at the temple. The dictionary notes the doctrine in the mechanism: God's worship is never priced out of reach of His poor. The vow is real, the valuation is real, and the priest is given discretion for exactly one purpose, which is to make sure poverty is no barrier to devotion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): POOR, adjective Wholly destitute of property, or not having competent means of subsistence. Comparative, poorer.
webster_full: POOR, adjective Wholly destitute of property, or not having property sufficient for a comfortable subsistence.
2. In a less strict sense, not rich; of small means.
3. Destitute of strength, beauty or dignity; barren; mean.
4. In Scripture, humble; in a state of dependence on God; poor in spirit.
POORLY, adverb Without wealth; in indigence; with little success.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The misreading to name is the prosperity one. Leviticus 27 is sometimes used to suggest that larger giving purchases larger standing before God. The chapter does the opposite: it fixes the valuations by divine appointment and then instructs the priest to assess the poor man according to his ability so that his vow is as acceptable as any other.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God has never priced access to Himself. Leviticus 12:8 let the poor bring birds instead of a lamb, and that is the offering Mary brought for the Lord of glory.

pos: adj. (comparative of rich; of greater wealth)
etymology: Saxon rice, powerful, wealthy, with the comparative ending. In Daniel 11:2 it renders a Hebrew word for great riches.
biblical_def: The angel gives Daniel a plain forecast of the Persian succession: “And now will I shew thee the truth. Behold, there shall stand up yet three kings in Persia; and the fourth shall be far richer than they all: and by his strength through his riches he shall stir up all against the realm of Grecia” (Daniel 11:2). The Authorized Version uses richer once, and it uses it of a king whose wealth is the engine of a war. His strength is through his riches; the treasury raises the army, and the army falls on Greece. Then the next verse turns the page: “And a mighty king shall stand up, that shall rule with great dominion, and do according to his will” (Daniel 11:3). The dictionary reads Daniel 11 as genuine predictive prophecy delivered to Daniel in the sixth century BC, not as a second-century composition written after the events — that reading is the critical hypothesis Daniel 11 was invented to explain away, and the dictionary rejects it. The chapter's point is the point of the whole book. Empires are rich, and then they are gone. The God of heaven sets up kings and removes kings, and He had told Daniel the sequence before any of them stood up.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): RICH, adjective Wealthy; opulent; possessing a large portion of land, goods or money. Comparative, richer.
webster_full: RICH, adjective Wealthy; opulent; possessing a large portion of land, goods or money, or a larger portion than is common to other men.
2. Having abundant materials for any thing; abundant in materials.
3. Splendid; costly; valuable; precious; sumptuous.
4. Fertile; fruitful; capable of producing large crops.
RICHES, noun Wealth; opulence; affluence; possessions of land, goods or money in abundance.

Dan 2:21

corruption_summary: Daniel 11 is widely dated after the events it predicts; the dictionary holds the sixth-century Daniel and genuine prophecy.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant academic treatment of Daniel 11 is that it is not prophecy at all but second-century history written as though foretold. That conclusion is required by the critical assumption that predictive prophecy of this precision cannot occur, not by any evidence in the text; the book presents itself as Daniel's, the Lord Jesus cites Daniel by name as a prophet, and the dictionary follows Him.

The principle to recover is Daniel 2:21. The chapter is not a list of kings for its own sake; it is a demonstration that He changeth the times and the seasons, removeth kings, and setteth up kings. The fourth Persian was far richer than them all, and his riches bought him a war and not a throne that lasted.

pos: adj. (comparative of tall; of greater height)
etymology: Welsh tal, high, lofty, with the comparative ending. In Deuteronomy 1:28 it renders a Hebrew word for height or loftiness.
biblical_def: Moses recalls the night Israel refused the land, and he quotes the spies' report back at them: “Whither shall we go up? our brethren have discouraged our heart, saying, The people is greater and taller than we; the cities are great and walled up to heaven; and moreover we have seen the sons of the Anakims there” (Deuteronomy 1:28). Every clause is a measurement — taller, greater, walled up to heaven — and every measurement is honest. The spies did not lie. Numbers 13:33 records what the measuring did to them: “and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Numbers 13:33). The Authorized Version uses taller once. The dictionary notes exactly where the unbelief lay. It was not in seeing the giants; Caleb saw them too. It was in leaving God out of the comparison. Moses' answer is the only answer: “Dread not, neither be afraid of them” (Deuteronomy 1:29), because the LORD your God goeth before you. A believer who measures the obstacle accurately and omits the Almighty has done arithmetic, not faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): TALL, adjective High in stature; long and comparatively slender; as a tall man. Comparative, taller.
webster_full: TALL, adjective High in stature; long and comparatively slender; as a tall man or tree.
2. High; lofty; as a tall tower.
3. Sturdy; lusty; bold; courageous.
TALLNESS, noun Height of stature; highness.
2. Height; as the tallness of a tree.

And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic reading makes Kadesh a failure of self-esteem: the Israelites felt like grasshoppers and needed to think better of themselves. Scripture calls it unbelief, and says so repeatedly — they believed not his word, they murmured, they rebelled against the commandment of the LORD. The cure was not a higher view of Israel but a true view of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that accurate measurement is not faith. The Anakim really were taller; the walls really were high. Caleb saw the same giants and said, let us go up at once, for we are well able. The difference between the two reports is one factor left out of the second.

pos: adj. (comparative of goodly; more comely in appearance)
etymology: From goodly, Saxon godlic, of good appearance, with the comparative ending. In 1 Samuel 9:2 it renders the Hebrew tob, good, used of outward form.
biblical_def: Saul is introduced by his looks: “And he had a son, whose name was Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly: and there was not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he: from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people” (1 Samuel 9:2). The Authorized Version uses goodlier once, and it uses it of the king Israel asked for. He was the handsomest man in the nation and a head taller than everybody else, which is precisely what a people who wanted a king like the other nations would choose. The whole tragedy of his reign is prefigured in the sentence, because nothing is said of his heart. The correction comes seven chapters later, when Samuel is sent to Bethlehem and begins to repeat the mistake: “Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). The dictionary reads the two verses together as one lesson. Saul was goodlier; David was ruddy and of a fair countenance and the youngest of eight, and he was the man after God's own heart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): GOODLY, adjective Being of a handsome form; beautiful; graceful; pleasant; agreeable. Comparative, goodlier.
webster_full: GOODLY, adjective Being of a handsome form; beautiful; graceful; as a goodly person; goodly raiment.
2. Pleasant; agreeable; desirable; as goodly days.
3. Bulky; swelling; affectedly turgid.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The one error worth naming is the modern inversion that treats beauty itself as a construct or an injustice. Scripture is quite comfortable saying that Saul was the handsomest man in Israel, that Rachel was beautiful, that David was of a fair countenance. It simply refuses to let appearance decide anything that matters.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is 1 Samuel 16:7. The LORD seeth not as man seeth. Israel asked for a king like all the nations and got the goodliest man in the land; God chose a shepherd boy, and the choosing is still the pattern for how He builds His church.

pos: adj. (comparative of happy; more blessed, better off)
etymology: From hap, chance or lot, with -y and the comparative ending. In 1 Corinthians 7:40 it renders the Greek makarios in its comparative force — more blessed.
biblical_def: Paul closes his chapter on marriage with a judgment about widows: “The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth; but if her husband be dead, she is at liberty to be married to whom she will; only in the Lord. But she is happier if she so abide, after my judgment: and I think also that I have the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 7:39-40). Three things are settled in two verses. She is free to remarry; she must marry only in the Lord; and in the apostle's judgment she is happier remaining as she is. The Authorized Version uses happier once. The word is not about cheerfulness. Paul has been arguing from the present distress and from undivided attention to the things of the Lord — the unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit. And the apostle's closing phrase is not diffidence: I think also that I have the Spirit of God is a claim to apostolic authority, not a disclaimer. The dictionary reads the chapter as Scripture presents it: marriage is honourable and good, celibacy is a gift not a rank, and the widow's liberty is real in both directions.

corruption_summary: The verse is pressed either into a ban on remarriage or into indifference about marrying in the Lord; Paul says neither.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome has used 1 Corinthians 7 to elevate celibacy into a higher state and to discourage the remarriage of widows; the dictionary rejects that reading, since Paul expressly says she is at liberty to be married to whom she will, and elsewhere directs that younger widows marry. The opposite error ignores the qualification Paul does impose: only in the Lord. A believing widow is free to remarry and is not free to marry an unbeliever.

The principle to recover is that both estates are gifts. Marriage is honourable in all, and the single life for the Lord's sake is a gift He gives to some. Paul gives his apostolic judgment that the widow is happier abiding, and grounds it in undivided care for the things of the Lord — not in any superiority of the unmarried over the married.

pos: adj. (comparative of narrow; of less breadth)
etymology: Saxon nearu, narrow, strait, with the comparative ending. In Isaiah 28:20 it renders a Hebrew verb meaning to be gathered up or too short.
biblical_def: Isaiah mocks the covenant Jerusalem had made with death — her treaty with Egypt, her refuge in lies — with the image of a bed that will not do: “For the bed is shorter than that a man can stretch himself on it: and the covering narrower than that he can wrap himself in it” (Isaiah 28:20). Anyone who has lain cold under a short blanket knows the proverb at once. A false refuge does not fail dramatically; it simply does not reach. You pull it up and your feet are out; you stretch out and your shoulders are bare. The Authorized Version uses narrower once, and this is the verse. Four verses earlier Isaiah had named the alternative: “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste” (Isaiah 28:16). The New Testament applies that stone to Christ. The dictionary reads the two images as the whole of Isaiah 28 in miniature: there is a bed too short, and there is a foundation that is sure, and every soul is lying on one or standing on the other.

webster_full: NARROW, adjective Of little breadth; not wide or broad; having little distance from side to side.
2. Of little extent; very limited; as a narrow sphere.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The one misuse to name is the devotional one that reads Isaiah 28:20 as a general lament about life's disappointments. The context is specific: Jerusalem had made a covenant with death and taken refuge in lies, and the short bed is her treaty. Any refuge that is not the stone laid in Zion is a covering too narrow to wrap in.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the contrast Isaiah draws. The false refuge is measured and found short; the sure foundation is a tried stone, and he that believeth shall not make haste. The New Testament names the stone, and there is no third option in the chapter.
roots_summary: Saxon nearu, narrow or strait; in Isaiah 28:20 the covering too narrow to wrap in — the measure of a false refuge.

Hebrew tsarar, to be narrow, cramped, gathered up too short.
Isaiah 28:20 is the only place the Authorized Version uses narrower.
The short bed and narrow covering picture Jerusalem's treaty with Egypt.
Isaiah 28:16 sets against it the tried stone laid in Zion.

pos: adj. (comparative of few; smaller in number)
etymology: Saxon feawe, few, with the comparative ending. In Numbers 33:54 it renders a Hebrew word for the small or diminished in number.
biblical_def: The land is to be divided by lot, and the lot is to be scaled to the size of the family: “And ye shall divide the land by lot for an inheritance among your families: and to the more ye shall give the more inheritance, and to the fewer ye shall give the less inheritance: every man's inheritance shall be in the place where his lot falleth; according to the tribes of your fathers ye shall inherit” (Numbers 33:54). Two principles are held together in one sentence, and they are not usually held together. The size of each inheritance was proportional — more to the many, less to the fewer. The location was by lot, which is to say by the hand of God and not by preference, bidding, or power. The Authorized Version uses fewer once. The same command stands at Numbers 26:54. The dictionary notes what this arrangement rules out. No tribe negotiated its portion; none could buy a better valley; and none could complain that a bigger family got more land, since the proportion was commanded. Equity in the measure, sovereignty in the placing — that is how God settled His people, and the proverb draws the conclusion: the lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The two misreadings pull opposite ways. One takes the proportional clause as a mandate for equalising outcomes generally; the other ignores it and reads the conquest as simple seizure. The text is precise: the measure was proportioned to the number of the family, and the place was fixed by lot, which Scripture everywhere treats as the LORD's disposing and not chance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is contentment with a lot that was not chosen. Proverbs 16:33 says the whole disposing is of the LORD, and the believer's portion — in land, in family, in gifts — is assigned by the same hand.
roots_summary: Saxon feawe, few; in Numbers 33:54 the smaller family receives the smaller inheritance, the place assigned by lot.
